title_en: What LPs Really Want From Venture Funds
title_zh: LP 到底想从风投基金要什么：对话 Lenora Capital 的 Rachel
subtitle_zh: 从记者到配置者，Rachel 谈风投对标、继任规划与自有媒体的未来。
description: What LPs Really Want From Venture Funds

turns.zh: 大牌好货，超值价格，这就是你选 Rack 的理由。欢迎收听 Swimming with Allocators，这档从 LP（有限合伙人）视角出发的风投播客。我是主播 Alexa Bins。

turns.en: And Ernest Sepp. You ready? Let's dive in. Rachel, thanks for being on Swimming with Alligators. It's a pleasure to get to talk to you, especially because of your very interesting background that we have a lot of respect for.
turns.zh: 还有 Ernest Sepp。准备好了吗？我们开始吧。Rachel，感谢你来上 Swimming with Allocators。非常高兴能和你聊聊，尤其是因为你那段很有意思、让我们非常敬佩的经历。

turns.en: But I wanted to start the conversation with you just kind of telling your origin story. You grew up outside of Seattle on a farm, like Superman.
turns.zh: 不过我想先从你的成长故事聊起。你在 Seattle 郊外的一个农场长大，简直像超人一样。

turns.en: And so it took paths through journalism, finance and now you're an allocator. So could you just walk us through kind of like your origin story?
turns.zh: 你先后走过新闻、金融这些路，如今成了一名配置者（allocator）。能不能带我们捋一捋你的成长经历？

turns.en: Yeah, it's funny. I grew up about, well, the bird flies is a different story than traffic. But I grew up towards Mount Rainier from downtown Seattle.
turns.zh: 好啊，说来有意思。我长大的地方，直线距离和实际开车距离完全是两码事。我家在从 Seattle 市中心往 Mount Rainier 方向那一带。

turns.en: Very small town called Ravenstale. There wasn't a high school there. We went to high school in like the larger suburbinary next to us. I worked on a horse ranch, friends and family boarded horses and had cows.
turns.zh: 一个很小的镇子，叫 Ravensdale。镇上连高中都没有，我们得去旁边更大的郊区镇上读高中。我在一个马场打工，亲友家还寄养马匹、养牛。

turns.en: And it was the whole nine yards. So very different from living in downtown and kind of pursuing this career path. But with that, I grew up with a tech family who worked remote before remote work was really even a thing pre-COVID and all of that.
turns.zh: 全套的农场生活都体验过。所以这跟住在市中心、走这条职业道路完全是两种人生。话虽如此，我成长在一个科技行业家庭，早在远程办公成为潮流、疫情出现之前，我父母就已经远程工作了。

turns.en: So I had some exposure to like what was happening in the city through my parents, which was obviously awesome and being here in Seattle through the tech boom of the early 2000s and Microsoft and whatnot was very exciting.
turns.zh: 所以透过父母，我对城里正在发生的事有一些接触，这当然很棒；在 Seattle 亲历 2000 年代初的科技繁荣、Microsoft 等等，也非常令人兴奋。

turns.en: And so I have a deep attachment to being here. So then I went to school in Utah, so Farm Town Part Two basically. And I went to the University of Utah in Salt Lake City and I started out in journalism.
turns.zh: 所以我对这里有很深的感情。后来我去 Utah 读书，基本上就是农场小镇生活第二部。我就读了 Salt Lake City 的 University of Utah，一开始学的是新闻。

turns.en: I thought I wanted to be a writer. I wrote for a couple of different publications while I was a high school student and then continued to do that throughout college.
turns.zh: 我以为自己想当作家。高中时我就给几家不同的刊物写稿，大学期间也一直坚持。

turns.en: And about halfway through, I finished that degree early and I had a very, very competitive spirit. And I was thinking about my career and thinking about how exciting it was to watch my parents' careers.
turns.zh: 大约读到一半，我提前修完了那个学位。我这个人非常好胜，当时就在思考自己的职业，也想到看着我父母的职业一路发展是多么令人兴奋。

turns.en: And I was like, I want to pursue something in a little bit of a different field. I'm OK being an uncomfortable conversation. I'm OK learning really fast and on the fly.
turns.zh: 我就想，我要去做一个稍微不同领域的事。我不怕处在让人不太自在的对话里，也乐意快速学习、边干边学。

turns.en: And I grew up around a lot of talk about money. So I was like investing. Sounds like a great place to start. And so I ended up adding on another major and pursuing that.
turns.zh: 而且我从小身边就充满关于钱的讨论。所以我想，投资听起来是个不错的起点。于是我加修了另一个专业，往这个方向走。

turns.en: And through a string of internships and all sorts of series of events, I landed in the alligator world. So I've touched a lot of different stuff.
turns.zh: 经过一连串实习和各种机缘巧合，我最终踏进了配置者（allocator）的世界。所以我接触过很多不同的东西。

turns.en: I've been in the startup. I've been in the RA world. I've been in senior housing development, doing real estate stuff. And then, obviously, I had the whole journalism era beforehand, which was all mostly investigative and crime reporting.
turns.zh: 我待过初创公司，做过 RA（研究助理）的工作，也做过养老住宅开发这类房地产的事。当然，在此之前我还有整整一段新闻时期，主要是调查报道和罪案报道。

turns.en: So I've really had my hand in a lot of different pools over the years. But very happy to have landed where I am now, for sure. That's so cool to hear the parallels between journalism and investing.
turns.zh: 所以这些年我真的涉猎过很多不同的领域。但我很高兴最终落到了现在这个位置，绝对是。——听到新闻和投资之间的这些共通之处，真是太有意思了。

turns.en: Like, we are asking questions constantly. And that's very similar. I've, similarly, I've compared notes with friends who read scripts for a living and are producers, you know, where they're like, which of these should we help bring to life?
turns.zh: 比如说，我们无时无刻不在提问，这一点非常相似。我也一样，我跟那些以读剧本为业、当制片人的朋友交流过心得，他们会说：这些项目里，哪一个值得我们帮忙搬上银幕？

turns.en: Do you, when you think about that journalism skill set, any advice for the rest of us on being better question askers? Or what can we learn from a journalist to be better investors?
turns.zh: 当你想到新闻这套技能时，有没有什么建议给我们这些人，帮我们成为更会提问的人？或者说，我们能从记者身上学到什么，来成为更好的投资人？

turns.en: Well, I think, well, there's two fold. One, I think about how journalism prepared me to work in investing just in the sense of being able to understand a person sitting across from you, figure out how to ask questions on the fly.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得有两方面。一方面，我在想新闻是怎么为我在投资行业工作做准备的——就在于你能读懂坐在你对面的这个人，懂得如何临场提问。

turns.en: I was always pretty anti, like, script questions. I would tell myself I was going to follow one and write it out, and it never ended up going that way.
turns.zh: 我一直挺排斥那种照着稿子念的问题。我总跟自己说要列一份提纲、写下来照着问，但最后从来都没能那样做。

turns.en: And I always found that to be for the better. And I think that being in that position, I'm sure you guys relate. Being in that position, I think, is you really how to dig in, how to follow up, how to figure out what's actually important to the person sitting across from you, because it's very hard to judge that before you really get the chance to talk to them.
turns.zh: 而且我发现那样反而更好。我想，处在那个位置——我相信你们也有同感——处在那个位置，才能真正学会怎么深挖、怎么追问，怎么弄清楚对面这个人真正在意的是什么，因为在真正有机会跟他们谈之前，这一点是很难判断的。

turns.en: So I mean, being an allocator is just interviewing over and over and over again. You can look at the numbers a million times and read through a deck a million times, but I feel like we end up making a majority of our decisions in a large way, influenced by, like, our conversations with people.
turns.zh: 所以说，做配置者其实就是一场接一场地面试。你可以把数字看上一百万遍、把 BP（融资演示稿）读上一百万遍，但我觉得我们最终做出的大多数决定，很大程度上都受到我们与人交谈的影响。

turns.en: So I think on one hand, it's not being afraid to ask really pointed, maybe uncomfortable questions. I think that's something that journalism taught me to be okay with, especially because in investigative and crime reporting, there's oftentimes people on the other side that don't really want to be talking to you.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，一方面是要敢于问出那种很尖锐、甚至可能让人不舒服的问题。这一点是新闻教会我坦然面对的，尤其因为在调查报道和罪案报道里，对面的人往往根本不想跟你谈。

turns.en: And so you get used to asking things that are maybe provoking or are not necessarily received well, but that's just part of the job. And then on the other hand, it's interesting now, in venture specifically from the allocator perspective, that we've kind of come full circle where on one hand, I credit a lot of my maybe like unique edge to having a past career in journalism, but now it's almost like the other side is merging over to with the whole new media concept.
turns.zh: 所以你会习惯去问一些可能带有挑衅、或者未必受欢迎的问题，但这本来就是工作的一部分。另一方面，现在有意思的是，具体到风投、从配置者的视角看，我们有点绕了一圈回到原点：一方面，我把我那种也许算得上独特的优势，归功于自己曾经做过新闻；但现在，随着整个新媒体概念的兴起，另一边似乎也在向新闻这一侧靠拢融合。

turns.en: Everybody has a sub-stack. Everybody has a podcast. So now they're so inherently intertwined that it's kind of, to an extent, you kind of need to know how to be a journalist a little bit in order to be an efficient investor at all.
turns.zh: 人人都有 Substack，人人都有播客。所以现在两者天然地深度交织在一起，某种程度上，你得稍微懂点怎么做记者，才能算得上一个高效的投资人。

turns.en: So I don't know, in a weird way, looking back, it was kind of an accident, but I would love to say it was intentional, but I think that the two fields really do cross over a ton and are more so as time goes on.
turns.zh: 所以我也说不准，回头看，这在某种奇怪意义上算是无心插柳，我倒真希望说这是有意为之。但我认为这两个领域确实大量交叉，而且随着时间推移交叉得越来越多。

turns.en: Yeah. And there's also a rich history of former journalists becoming successful venture capitalists. So it has happened. And I've always felt like my background in equity research was the more of a financial journalist for a financial institution.
turns.zh: 是啊。而且前记者转型成为成功风险投资家的历史也很丰富，所以这种事确实发生过。我一直觉得，我做股票研究（equity research）的背景，更像是给一家金融机构当财经记者。

turns.en: So just learning how to find what is the true value, what's the truth, is what you're trying to find in those roles. Andrew Chen, Jason Calicanus, Josh, Paul Merlucky, who founded Andrew, a major journalism in college, which always makes me laugh.
turns.zh: 所以在那些岗位上，你要学着去找到什么是真正的价值、什么是真相。Andrew Chen、Jason Calacanis、Josh Paul，还有那位大学主修新闻的 Mike Maples——这一点总让我觉得好笑。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Mike Maples. So yeah, there's a history of that. Because you brought it up, what are some of your favorite questions to ask fund managers?
turns.zh: 对、对、对，Mike Maples。所以是的，这方面是有先例的。既然你提到了，那你最喜欢问基金经理的一些问题是什么？

turns.en: That you feel like really dig into that person and get you an answer that you feel like you wouldn't have got if you just asked your scripted, hey, what is your portfolio construction?
turns.zh: 就是那种能真正深挖对方、让你得到答案的问题——那种答案是你如果只是照着稿子问「嘿，你的组合构建是怎样的」所得不到的。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I like to dig in and get detailed if I'm talking to a team. It obviously depends on the difference between a mega-mega fund manager and an emerging manager, because I would say from a general overview, I spend most of my time on either end of that spectrum.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，如果我在跟一个团队谈，我喜欢深挖、抠细节。这当然取决于超大型基金管理人（mega fund）和新兴管理人（emerging manager）之间的差别，因为总体来看，我的时间大多花在这个光谱的两端。

turns.en: And so the questions that you ask are going to be different at the end of the day. And the smaller, more emerging managers are easier to dig into because they are more eager to answer your questions, and they do have an interest in proving themselves, whereas you find the opposite, right, with the big guys that if they don't want to answer something, they're not going to do it, which is just a reality.
turns.zh: 所以你最终问的问题会不一样。规模更小、更新兴的管理人更容易深挖，因为他们更愿意回答你的问题，也确实有证明自己的动力；而对那些大牌机构，你会发现恰恰相反——如果他们不想回答某个问题，他们就不会答，这就是现实。

turns.en: And so with smaller fund managers, I think that sourcing is really something that is easy to give a very blanket answer to. Like, yes, fantastic, you attend events, you have a good network from whatever large company you worked at prior to this, like, that's an obvious give.
turns.zh: 所以对较小的基金管理人来说，我觉得项目来源（sourcing）这件事很容易给出一个非常笼统的答案。比如：很好，你参加活动，你在此前工作的那家大公司积累了不错的人脉——这显然是明摆着的。

turns.en: But getting down even into the like, you know, what is your unique edge? How are you using media to help you? What is your IRL presence like?
turns.zh: 但要真正往下深挖，比如：你独特的优势是什么？你怎么利用媒体来帮自己？你线下（IRL）的存在感如何？

turns.en: I think the community building has become a huge thing, but like, let's go beyond that sort of buzzword and talk about what you're doing, like, pull up your calendar and let's talk about what you've done this week, last week, whatever.
turns.zh: 我觉得社群建设（community building）已经成了一件大事，但我们不妨超越那种流行词，谈谈你到底在做什么——比如把你的日历调出来，我们聊聊你这周、上周都做了些什么，诸如此类。

turns.en: I'm sure also the experience as a journalist of getting background and, you know, in back channeling feel pretty much similar. Talk to us about like your journalism career has prepared you for like finding background, back channeling on, hey, is it actually congruent of what you say you do and help?
turns.zh: 我相信你做记者时那种做背景调查、走后门渠道（back channeling）的经验也很相似。跟我们讲讲，你的新闻生涯是怎么为你做准备，让你能去查背景、走渠道核实——嘿，这跟你嘴上说的到底一不一致，从而帮上忙的？

turns.en: Does the actual market feel that way? Yeah. Oh my gosh. This is my favorite topic. I did a ton, a ton, a ton of public records requesting when I was doing journalism because in crime and investigative stuff, there is a ton of information that is technically publicly available, but is behind different kinds of FOIA walls and whatnot.
turns.zh: 实际市场是不是也这么看？——是啊，天哪，这可是我最爱的话题。我做新闻时申请了海量海量的公共记录，因为在罪案和调查报道里，有大量信息在法律意义上是公开的，却被挡在各种 FOIA（信息自由法）门槛之类后面。

turns.en: And that process can be a huge pain to navigate. It is not only on a federal level governed by FOIA, but then state by state, there are different laws that govern what has to be publicly released and how.
turns.zh: 而这个流程走起来可以非常痛苦。它不只是在联邦层面由 FOIA 管辖，各个州还有各自不同的法律，规定哪些必须公开、以什么方式公开。

turns.en: So when I was living in Utah, it was the grandma system. Here it's the Washington state public record system. And the way that you request information is super, super, super specific.
turns.zh: 所以我住在 Utah 时用的是那套 GRAMA（犹他州政府记录调取法）系统，在这里则是 Washington 州的公共记录系统。而你申请信息的方式超级、超级、超级具体。

turns.en: If you mess up in your request, you can be set back a month, but there is so much information that is publicly available by law, but your actual access to it is blocked by the request process.
turns.zh: 如果你的申请写错一点，可能就白白耽误一个月。但有太多信息依法是公开的，只是你实际获取它的路径被申请流程给卡住了。

turns.en: So doing that in journalism was huge because I figured out how to navigate it, how you needed to talk to people, who you needed to get on the phone and yell at to say, it's been 30 days.
turns.zh: 所以在做新闻时练这套本事非常关键，因为我摸清了怎么在其中周旋、怎么跟人打交道、该给谁打电话吼一句：都 30 天了。

turns.en: I need to move on to the next step in this process. Like this is how this works. And so it's as simple as like there's an online portal where you can go and request different information from your government that pertains to public employers, private employers, tons of different stuff that's processed, reported on financially, tons of stuff in the tax universe that can all be really good indications about what's happening, maybe in a certain market,
turns.zh: 我得推进到流程的下一步了，就是这么运作的。所以其实很简单：有一个在线门户，你可以在上面向政府申请各种信息，涉及公共雇主、私人雇主，大量经过处理、有财务报告的内容，还有税务领域里的大量资料，这些都能很好地指示某个市场也许正在发生什么，

turns.en: maybe with a certain firm. And so it serves as a good way to background check, not necessarily people individually, but like a group and what they're doing.
turns.zh: 或者某家公司正在发生什么。所以它是一种很好的背景调查方式——不一定是针对某个人，而是针对一个群体以及他们在做的事。

turns.en: And so learning how to navigate that process early on and be able to step in doing that has been awesome. We use FOIA to get a fold of all kinds of endowment and pension planning, investing strategies and to see how they've changed over time, because all that has to be publicly filed.
turns.zh: 所以早早学会怎么在这个流程里周旋、能够上手去做，这一直很棒。——我们会用 FOIA 去调取各种捐赠基金（endowment）和养老金的规划、投资策略，看它们随时间如何变化，因为这些都必须在公开备案。

turns.en: That's a very cool example of why your families and clients need Rachel. Like this layer that you are providing at Lenora. It's a little bit untraditional.
turns.zh: 这就是一个很酷的例子，说明了你的家族客户为什么需要 Rachel，也就是你在 Lenora 提供的这一层服务，它有点不走寻常路。

turns.en: Do you mind explaining to those who don't know about Lenora what your platform does and where you sit? Yeah. So Lenora Capital is the private investments arm of Brighton Jones.
turns.zh: 你介不介意给不了解 Lenora 的人解释一下，你们的平台是做什么的、你处在什么位置？——好啊。Lenora Capital 是 Brighton Jones 的私募投资部门。

turns.en: And so Brighton Jones is a really massive RIA based here in Seattle where I'm sitting, but we've got offices all over the country, 30 billion in assets, 4,000 clients, think traditional private wealth management.
turns.zh: Brighton Jones 是一家规模非常庞大的 RIA（注册投资顾问），总部就在我所在的 Seattle，但我们在全美各地都有办公室，管理 300 亿美元资产、服务 4000 位客户，你可以理解为传统的私人财富管理。

turns.en: And then over time, we've built out a very dedicated family office platform that is really separate from the rest of the wealth management business, because I mean, over the last 25 years of existing, especially being headquartered here in Seattle, as you can imagine, there was some serious, serious wealth accumulated with some of our early, early clients.
turns.zh: 随着时间推移，我们又搭建了一个非常专门的家族办公室（family office）平台，它跟财富管理业务的其他部分基本是分开的。因为我是说，在成立的这 25 年里，尤其是总部设在 Seattle，你可以想象，我们一些非常早期的客户积累了相当相当可观的财富。

turns.en: So we have tons of family office clients that range from C-suite to legal to high up at public and private companies that, at the end of the day, need a completely different specialized set of planning tools.
turns.zh: 所以我们有大量家族办公室客户，从企业高管（C-suite）、法律界人士，到上市公司和私营公司的高层，他们说到底需要一整套完全不同的、专门的规划工具。

turns.en: So we've developed a trust company that exists within us. We have a fantastic tax team. We have a state lawyers. It's the full nine yards. And so family office operates differently because at the end of the day, they have a huge amount of capital and a lot of them have both a financial interest, but also a personal interest in investing privately.
turns.zh: 所以我们内部设立了一家信托公司，有一支出色的税务团队，还有遗产律师（estate lawyers），一应俱全。家族办公室的运作方式不一样，因为说到底，他们手握巨额资本，而且很多人既有财务上的兴趣、也有个人层面对私募投资的兴趣。

turns.en: As you can imagine, if you are the CEO of a massive publicly traded company, you're going to get a lot of unique opportunities to be an LP in a fund or put money towards a startup, but at the end of the day, you as a single person off of your own private balance sheet cannot operate like a fund manager when you've got a company to run.
turns.zh: 你可以想象，如果你是一家大型上市公司的 CEO，你会得到很多独特的机会去做一只基金的 LP，或者往初创公司投钱；但说到底，你作为一个个体、用自己的私人资产负债表，在你还有一家公司要经营的情况下，是没法像基金管理人那样运作的。

turns.en: And so we built out Lenore Capital three years ago, roughly, brought in a bunch of awesome people to basically run a drawdown fund of our own that Capital is committed to by these different families.
turns.zh: 所以大约三年前我们组建了 Lenora Capital，请来一批非常优秀的人，基本上就是运营一只我们自己的抽用式基金（drawdown fund），资本由这些不同的家族承诺出资。

turns.en: So we invest in venture. We invest in real estate. We invest in private equity. We do stuff directly and through funds. So we are an LP on the venture side exclusively, private equity deals, buyouts, and real estate.
turns.zh: 我们投资风投、投资房地产、投资私募股权，既做直接投资也通过基金投资。所以在风投这一侧，我们完全以 LP 身份参与；私募股权交易、并购（buyout）和房地产也是。

turns.en: We'll do direct deals with venture wheel and outsource to the experts. So that's kind of how our firm operates. We bring money from our clients.
turns.zh: 风投方面我们既直接做交易，也会外包给专家。我们公司大致就是这么运作的：我们把客户的钱汇集起来。

turns.en: We don't really have to fundraise, I think, is an important way to think about it. So we have an ongoing series of vehicles so that there's something open for people that want to re-up and recommit in order to maintain their allocation of privates.
turns.zh: 我觉得，一个重要的理解角度是：我们其实不必去募资。所以我们有一系列持续开放的载体（vehicle），让那些想续投、想重新承诺以维持其私募配置比例的人随时有可投的东西。

turns.en: But it's not a fundraising environment, which makes it really unique. Walk me through your own personal kind of journey with like understanding the asset class venture.
turns.zh: 但这并不是一个募资环境，这让一切非常独特。——带我们讲讲你自己理解风投这个资产类别的个人历程吧。

turns.en: Like it's not something that you can just, you can read headlines and it'd be stale already. So just curious how you were able to figure out, all right, what are the right channels?
turns.zh: 这不是那种你光读读 headlines 就够的东西——等你读完，信息就已经过时了。所以很好奇你是怎么弄明白：好，哪些才是对的信息渠道？

turns.en: What's really going on? Yeah. Well, it's interesting because I think the growing up in a tech universe, you have a very generic idea of what that means.
turns.zh: 到底真正在发生什么？——是啊。嗯，这很有意思，因为我觉得在科技圈里长大，你对这一切意味着什么只有一个很笼统的概念。

turns.en: What is a venture capitalist? What is this asset class? Obviously, the 2000s are nothing like what we're living in now. I worked at a VC back startup when I was in college, which was kind of a helpful introduction to what does it mean to be on the other side of this table.
turns.zh: 风险投资家是什么？这个资产类别是什么？显然，2000 年代跟我们如今所处的环境完全不一样。我大学时在一家有风投背景的初创公司工作过，那段经历算是很有帮助的入门，让我明白坐在这张桌子另一边意味着什么。

turns.en: And that was the first time that I ever had any personal interaction with venture dollars and what does it mean to be beholden to investors and have things to deal with in terms of having outside capital.
turns.zh: 那是我第一次切身接触到风投的钱，也是第一次体会到受制于投资人、因为拿了外部资本而要面对各种事情是什么滋味。

turns.en: So that was kind of another entry point into, okay, this is super interesting. These people have such an interesting approach to investing. There is huge risk in what they're doing, but obviously huge potential reward.
turns.zh: 所以那算是又一个切入点，让我觉得：好，这太有意思了。这些人做投资的方式非常有趣，他们做的事有巨大风险，但显然也有巨大的潜在回报。

turns.en: And then developing this whole sort of institutional platform approach is a completely different story because, I mean, we've had access to some of the most incredible managers, which has been awesome, because when you start as an LP and you are not in a massive, massive and download-sized LP, you wonder, okay, well, some of these firms are impossible to get into.
turns.zh: 而后再去搭建这一整套机构化的平台打法，就完全是另一回事了。因为我是说，我们接触到了极其出色的一批管理人，这非常棒；因为当你刚开始做 LP、又不是那种超大规模、捐赠基金级别（endowment-sized）的 LP 时，你会犯嘀咕：好吧，有些机构根本挤不进去。

turns.en: Some of them are notoriously just never going to accept new LP that they aren't familiar with. How long is it going to take us to get access to some of these firms?
turns.zh: 有些机构是出了名的、绝不会接受他们不熟悉的新 LP。那我们要花多久才能进入其中一些机构？

turns.en: And thankfully, and I think in large part, our huge client base that has a lot of resources to provide, but also just who we work with, it's been a lot easier than we thought to be able to get access to these managers, which has been great.
turns.zh: 值得庆幸的是，我认为很大程度上要归功于我们庞大的客户群——他们能提供大量资源，也在于我们合作的对象本身——所以要接触到这些管理人比我们原本想的容易得多，这一点非常好。

turns.en: And then it's allowed us to actually take a really strategic approach to, okay, we're not just going to say yes because it's this brand's name, but now we have this slew of brand names to be able to compare and benchmark against one another.
turns.zh: 这也让我们能够真正采取一种很有策略性的做法：好，我们不会仅仅因为是某个大牌的名字就点头，而是现在手上有这么一批大牌，可以拿来相互比较、相互对标（benchmark）。

turns.en: We actually are in a really great position of choice. And so, learning about venture from an LP perspective really directly is so different because I don't directly come from the tech world and my background is financial.
turns.zh: 我们其实处在一个非常有选择权的好位置。所以直接从 LP 的视角去了解风投是非常不同的体验，因为我并不直接来自科技圈，我的背景是金融。

turns.en: It's such a different experience from being like, okay, and we invest primarily in the tech and tech-associated venture universe. And so, we're coming at it from a really, really, really mathematical perspective.
turns.zh: 这跟那种「好，我们主要投科技及科技相关的风投圈」的人是完全不同的体验。所以我们是从一个非常非常非常偏数学（量化）的角度切入的。

turns.en: We're coming at it to hold into investors that are on a shorter timeline. And just the allocator universe is different from the tech universe, but they're merged so closely.
turns.zh: 我们切入时要顾及的是那些时间线更短的投资者。而且配置者（allocator）的圈子跟科技圈不一样，但两者又融合得非常紧密。

turns.en: So, I think that learning about venture from this perspective has been so different because it's kind of, it's been outside of the echo chamber of Silicon Valley is probably the best way to put it.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得从这个视角去了解风投非常不一样，因为——最贴切的说法大概是——它一直在 Silicon Valley 那个回音室（echo chamber）之外。

turns.en: So, I think that I've had a little bit more of a practical experience kind of figuring out how we feel about the asset class, which I think has been helpful, but it's been really exciting to see kind of how it's developed and how our access has developed over the last couple of years.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，在摸索我们对这个资产类别的看法时，我多了一点更务实的经验，我想这是有帮助的；但看到过去几年它如何发展、我们的触达渠道如何发展，也确实令人兴奋。

turns.en: This benchmarking topic is fascinating one. You've said you spend a lot of your time on sort of like the barbell, the top tier funds as well as the emerging managers.
turns.zh: 对标这个话题很有意思。你说过你很多时间都花在那个「杠铃（barbell）」两端——顶级基金以及新兴管理人上。

turns.en: Focusing on these top tier funds, can you walk us through how you assess them and benchmark them against each other? Yeah, it's incredibly challenging because you do not have a consistent flow of data at the end of the day.
turns.zh: 聚焦这些顶级基金，你能带我们讲讲你是怎么评估它们、怎么把它们相互对标的吗？——是啊，这极具挑战，因为说到底你并没有一个持续一致的数据流。

turns.en: There is very un-uniform reporting that happens with these top tier managers that are just not beholden to proving themselves. There's great data providers out there, which we have access to and we use, but when you have different fund vintages and you have different specialties, you have different verticals, maybe your front operates in a different way, you classify late stage differently than the next guy.
turns.zh: 这些顶级管理人的报告非常不统一，他们根本不需要去证明自己。市面上有很棒的数据供应商，我们能拿到也在用，但当你面对不同的基金年份（vintage）、不同的专长、不同的垂直领域，也许你的前端运作方式不同、你对后期（late stage）的划分跟别人也不一样。

turns.en: Using benchmarking is, I think, really important to understand, can this firm return capital to its investors and hasn't been able to do it consistently?
turns.zh: 我觉得用对标来搞清楚一件事非常重要：这家机构能不能把钱返还给它的投资人，而且能不能持续做到这一点？

turns.en: Like, that's number one, obviously. And so, being able to see, I mean, at the end of the day, DPI is really, really important when we don't have a perpetual timeline.
turns.zh: 这显然是第一位的。所以，能够看到——我是说，说到底，当我们没有无限期的时间线时，DPI（投入资本分红率）真的非常非常重要。

turns.en: So we think about an endowment who is just trying to keep this pool of capital growing for forever, hypothetically. We have families and real people that have goals that they want to meet at the end of the day, whether it's them or their children or whatever.
turns.zh: 你想想捐赠基金，它（假设）只是想永远让这一池资本不断增值。而我们面对的是家族和真实的人，他们说到底有想要实现的目标，无论是为了他们自己、他们的孩子还是别的什么。

turns.en: So we can't be thinking about 30 years in the future and exits that are going to happen off of continuation vehicles and things like that. We have to find managers that are going to be able to generate DPI.
turns.zh: 所以我们不能去想着 30 年后的未来、想着靠延续基金（continuation vehicle）之类来实现的退出。我们必须找到那些能够产生 DPI 的管理人。

turns.en: That's incredibly important. So that's a metric that we look at a ton, obviously, and focus on. But a lot of it, I think, is very intangible in the sense of, how do you benchmark somebody's media strategy against another?
turns.zh: 这一点极其重要。所以这显然是我们大量关注、重点看的一个指标。但我觉得其中很多东西是非常无形的，比如：你要怎么把某个人的媒体策略跟另一个人对标？

turns.en: There's, I mean, you could benchmark generated views and engagement and interaction across different social platforms, but what does that really tell you?
turns.zh: 我是说，你确实可以对标在不同社交平台上产生的浏览量、互动和参与度，但那到底能告诉你什么？

turns.en: I think a lot of the benchmarking is a little bit of a finger to the wind. And it's trying to figure out how do you compare all of the unique strategies that these top peer venture managers employ against one another, because they're all really different.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多对标工作有点像是「把手指举起来测风向」、凭感觉判断。它就是要设法搞清楚：这些顶级风投管理人各自采用的独特策略，你要怎么把它们相互比较，因为它们真的都很不一样。

turns.en: And so there's tactical benchmarking, and then there is a person-to-person sort of subjective benchmarking that has to happen with what's everything outside of what you can put on a spreadsheet.
turns.zh: 所以有战术层面的对标，还有一种人与人之间的、主观的对标，它针对的是所有没法放进电子表格里的东西。

turns.en: And that's, I think, just increasingly becoming a more important part of the process of making these decisions. Now we're going to take a quick break to speak with our sponsor.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得，这在做出这些决定的过程中正变得越来越重要。——好，现在我们稍微休息一下，跟我们的赞助商聊几句。

turns.en: What's an issue you've been helping a founder client with lately? Good question. So there's a few, I'll give you kind of two that are popping up all the time.
turns.zh: 最近你在帮一位创始人客户处理什么问题？——好问题。有几个，我给你讲两个最近特别常冒出来的。

turns.en: So I would say one that comes up quite a lot for me lately, interestingly enough, even though I'm not an employment lawyer, although we have a very exciting employment law group, is the kind of a disagreement or a separation of one of the founders and a company.
turns.zh: 我会说，最近经常找上我的一个问题——有意思的是，尽管我不是劳动法律师（不过我们有一个非常出色的劳动法团队）——就是某位创始人与公司之间的分歧或分道扬镳。

turns.en: And this has been happening earlier and earlier in the lives of companies, and frankly has gotten to a point where I now tell clients that when they're raising their first round, they say, hey, is it a problem that we've had this third co-founder that's not with us anymore?
turns.zh: 而且这种情况在公司生命周期里出现得越来越早，坦白说已经到了这种地步：现在客户在融第一轮时会问我，嘿，我们曾有一位第三联合创始人、如今已经不在了，这会是个问题吗？

turns.en: And the answer is, no, actually, this happens all the time now. And I don't think that your investors are going to care particularly about the fact that a third investor is not here as long as it was handled correctly with advice of counsel and negotiated appropriately.
turns.zh: 我的回答是：不会，其实这种情况现在非常常见。我不认为你的投资人会特别在意有一位联合创始人不在了，只要当时在法律顾问的建议下正确处理、妥善谈判过就行。

turns.en: Our employment law group is working with me very closely. Rebecca, who's been on some of your podcasts, is probably getting tired of phone calls from me, but it's a very kind of busy potent area lately, and I've been guiding a lot of companies through that, and sometimes with the board involvement.
turns.zh: 我们的劳动法团队和我合作得非常紧密。Rebecca（她上过你们的一些播客）大概都接我电话接烦了，但这块最近非常繁忙、也很棘手，我一直在指导很多公司走过这一关，有时候还需要董事会介入。

turns.en: And the other one I'll give you a real quick one is, these days, AI and data is all the rage, so I am involved in so many discussions about licensing, selling, transferring data between companies, AI labs, vice versa, or AI labs and other AI labs, and all the exciting issues that come with that, data privacy, commercial considerations and indemnifications and so on that we get in the weeds on.
turns.zh: 另一个我快速讲一下：如今 AI 和数据正当红，所以我参与了大量关于数据授权、出售、在公司之间、AI 实验室之间、或 AI 实验室与其他 AI 实验室之间转移数据的讨论，还有随之而来的一切棘手问题——数据隐私、商业考量、赔偿条款（indemnification）等等，我们都要抠得很细。

turns.en: And you, at Sidley, are a liaison of AI internally, I understand. In the AI era, has that changed how you're working? Absolutely. It's really transformed the way I'm working in the kind of minutiae of day to day.
turns.zh: 而且我了解到，你在 Sidley 内部是 AI 联络人。在 AI 时代，这改变了你的工作方式吗？——当然。它真的彻底改变了我日常工作中那些细枝末节的方式。

turns.en: So I tell my clients when I theoretically boot up my computer every morning, although I never turn it off. The two apps that I open immediately are my Outlook and then ChatGPT.
turns.zh: 所以我跟我的客户说，理论上我每天早上开电脑——尽管我从不关机——我立刻打开的两个应用就是 Outlook，然后是 ChatGPT。

turns.en: And now, by the way, we kind of go back and forth, Claude, ChatGPT and other tools, so we're not, you know, we're agnostic to the tools, whichever one's better.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，现在我们会在 Claude、ChatGPT 和其他工具之间来回切换，所以我们并不绑定某个工具，哪个更好用就用哪个。

turns.en: But the idea is that from the first minute that I log in, it is there as an assistant to what I do. It is empowering me. I am able to do what used to take, you know, five billable hours in maybe five minutes now.
turns.zh: 但核心理念是：从我登录的第一分钟起，它就在那里，充当我工作的助手，为我赋能。以前可能要花五个计费小时（billable hours）才能做完的事，现在我大概五分钟就能搞定。

turns.en: Incredible. It is absolutely incredible, so I'm able to do more work that way. At the same time, you know, it has not taken away any of what I think is my value add, which is the experience, the human touch, the practicality and being able to guide a client through a very sophisticated, you know, transaction, you know, negotiation and so on.
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。它确实不可思议，这样我就能做更多工作。与此同时，它并没有夺走任何我认为属于我的价值加分项——也就是经验、人情味、务实，以及能够引导客户走过一场非常复杂的交易、谈判等等。

turns.en: What has taken away is, hey, you know, I go to a board meeting now, I have an agent that drafts my board minutes, I can send those right after the board meeting, I don't need to ask an associate, I don't need to worry about the time that it takes them, I don't need to worry about writing off that time on the bill.
turns.zh: 它替我省掉的，是这些：嘿，我现在去参加董事会会议，我有一个 AI 智能体（agent）帮我起草董事会会议纪要，会后马上就能发出去，我不用去麻烦一位初级律师（associate），不用担心他们要花多少时间，也不用担心在账单上核销掉那段时间。

turns.en: And so all of that stuff, frankly, you know, and this is the interesting part that we hear from clients is they say, well, you know, you guys have all this AI, and how come, you know, your profits are still so healthy and illegal in this, you know, the answer is because we can actually do a lot more, but on an individual basis, we're able to do things quicker and more efficiently and we see that and we are, you know, working hard to communicate to clients
turns.zh: 所以坦白讲，所有这些——而从客户那里听到的有意思的一点是，他们会说：你们有这么多 AI，怎么利润还这么健康？答案是：因为我们实际上能做的事多了很多，而且就个人而言，我们能更快、更高效地完成工作，我们看到了这一点，也在努力向客户传达：

turns.en: that they can see the kind of cost savings passed on to them. Yeah. You're getting Mike Plus. And now back to our LP interview. I was curious on how do you assess talent in the two different kind of barbells, right, size of the barbell, right, from when you're at a large firm, it seems like you're more like an NFL team, you have this big brand and it's moving.
turns.zh: 让他们看到省下的成本传递到了他们身上。好，现在回到我们的 LP 访谈。我很好奇，在这两种不同的「杠铃」上、也就是杠铃的不同规模上，你是怎么评估人才的？当你在一家大型机构时，你更像一支 NFL 球队，有着这个大品牌，而且它在不断运转。

turns.en: And then when you're at emerging manager, you're more of a tennis pro, where you're just individual going to these tournaments and assess just on your merits.
turns.zh: 而当你在一个新兴管理人那里，你更像一名网球职业选手，你是一个人去参加这些巡回赛，完全凭你自己的本事接受评判。

turns.en: How do you in your mind, how are you able to assess talent in those two different arenas? Yeah. I love the NSL Tennis Pro comparison. I think that's such a perfect way to put it.
turns.zh: 在你看来，你怎么能在这两个不同的赛场里评估人才？——是啊，我太喜欢这个「NFL 对网球职业选手」的比喻了，我觉得这个说法再贴切不过。

turns.en: It's obviously completely different. At the end of the day, the big brands can win talent because who doesn't want that name on their cap table sort of concept, which I think is ever present.
turns.zh: 这当然完全不同。说到底，大牌机构能赢得人才，因为谁不想让那个名字出现在自己的股权结构表（cap table）上呢？我觉得这种心态是无处不在的。

turns.en: I do think that there is still really important relationship building that happens there in the sense that some founders are going to pick a firm to be on their cap table because of the brand.
turns.zh: 我确实认为，那里仍然有非常重要的关系建立在进行——有些创始人会因为品牌而选择某家机构进入自己的股权结构表。

turns.en: Some people have a really close relationship with a particular partner. So I think that both of those things can be true when it comes to a household name that everybody recognizes.
turns.zh: 有些人则跟某一位合伙人关系非常密切。所以我觉得，当谈到一个人人皆知的招牌名字时，这两件事可以同时成立。

turns.en: Maybe you're going with them because they have fantastic resources and you want that brand association. Sometimes you're going with them because you have a relationship with a particular partner that you really trust.
turns.zh: 也许你选他们，是因为他们有极好的资源、你想要那种品牌关联；有时你选他们，是因为你跟某位你非常信任的合伙人有交情。

turns.en: You really want to be part of your team. Those two things can be true at the same time. On the smaller end, I think that you're pretty much entirely relying on the latter, which is that when the brand necessarily doesn't hold significant weight, you are picking the firm because of the person and you are picking the firm because of the partner that you want to work with.
turns.zh: 你真的很想成为他们团队的一部分。这两件事可以同时成立。而在规模较小的那一端，我觉得你几乎完全依赖后者：当品牌不一定有足够分量时，你选这家机构是因为那个人，是因为你想与之共事的那位合伙人。

turns.en: Assessing that talent is all about who is this person's network? Where do they come from? If they're starting a new fund, maybe they're in that sub $150 million range.
turns.zh: 评估这种人才，全靠这些问题：这个人的人脉是谁？他们从哪里来？如果他们在募一只新基金，也许规模在 1.5 亿美元以下那一档。

turns.en: It's like why you as a GP, where you come from, is it because you have an incredible network through a large tech company that you worked at?
turns.zh: 也就是说，你作为 GP（普通合伙人），你的出身背景是什么：是因为你曾在一家大型科技公司工作、从而拥有惊人的人脉吗？

turns.en: Is it because you've started something of your own and it was really successful and so you have great relationships with follow-on investors?
turns.zh: 是因为你自己创办过某个非常成功的项目，所以你跟后续轮投资人（follow-on investors）关系很好吗？

turns.en: Is it because of your academic background and the way that you're still heavily involved as an alumni? I think that from the founder perspective and the LP perspective, you're going to look at that person really differently and say, this has to fall on you because without a brand that is immediately recognizable, you as the individual are the super connector.
turns.zh: 是因为你的学术背景，以及你作为校友仍然深度参与其中吗？我觉得无论从创始人视角还是 LP 视角，你都会非常不同地看待这个人，并说：这一切都得落在你身上，因为没有一个一眼就能认出的品牌，你这个人本身就是那个「超级连接者」。

turns.en: You're the person that's helping us with distribution. You're the person that's helping us grow. You're the person that's going to help us bring really excellent follow-on capital onto this if you can't provide it.
turns.zh: 你是帮我们做分发的人，是帮我们成长的人，是那个会帮我们引入极其优秀的后续资本的人——如果你自己提供不了这笔钱的话。

turns.en: The talent part is so much more personal, I think, when it comes to a smaller general partner than it is when it comes to the really, really big guys.
turns.zh: 我觉得，比起那些非常非常大的机构，「人才」这件事在规模较小的普通合伙人身上要个人化得多。

turns.en: It doesn't mean it's not important on that end of the spectrum as well, but assessing talent is way more individual and they can have all of those great things like a newsletter like a media presence, but at the end of the day, it's all focused on them and they are the center of that universe.
turns.zh: 这并不意味着在光谱的另一端它就不重要，只是评估人才要个体化得多。他们也可以拥有那些很棒的东西，比如新闻通讯（newsletter）、媒体存在感，但说到底，一切都聚焦在他们本人身上，他们就是那个宇宙的中心。

turns.en: You mentioned that there are firms that you would have been surprised to say no to a few years ago or the reverse is true and without naming names.
turns.zh: 你提到过，有些机构如果放在几年前，你会对拒绝他们感到意外——或者反过来也成立——我们不点名。

turns.en: I'm curious, what's changed your mind in some cases about some of these brand name managers? Yeah, I think something huge that has developed a lot in the last couple of years is the idea of a real lack of succession planning.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，在某些情况下，是什么改变了你对这些大牌管理人的看法？——是啊，我觉得过去几年里凸显出来的一件大事，就是真正缺乏继任规划（succession planning）这个问题。

turns.en: When it comes to some of these major firms, especially if you have incredible partners that do attract a lot of people because they've built, if you're a mightest list investor that is an ideal person for people to work with and your network is a core piece of the business, especially if the firm is 20, 30 years old and you've been building it from day one, the day that you're not there anymore, there is going to be a difference because
turns.zh: 对一些大型机构来说尤其如此：如果你有非常出色的合伙人，他们确实能吸引很多人，因为如果你是那种上了「权力榜」（Midas List）的投资人，就是大家理想中想共事的对象，而你的人脉又是这门生意的核心一环——尤其当这家机构已经有 20、30 年历史、你从第一天起就在搭建它——那么当你不再在这里的那一天，一切就会不一样，因为

turns.en: the brand does do a lot of the pulling, obviously, but there is that relationship piece that still does exist with the mega funds because you can't have one over the other completely.
turns.zh: 品牌显然做了很多牵引工作，但在这些超大型基金里，关系那一环依然存在，因为你不可能完全让一方压倒另一方。

turns.en: You really need to develop both and maintain both and so I think that it can be a little bit concerning sometimes to see, okay, well, you've got this incredible track record.
turns.zh: 你真的需要同时发展并维护这两者。所以我觉得，有时看到这种情况会有点令人担忧：好吧，你有这样出色的过往业绩，

turns.en: You're doing great. You're raising the biggest fund you've ever had. It's 10 years with, God knows, five, six, seven, one year extension periods.
turns.zh: 你干得很好，正在募集你史上最大的一只基金，期限 10 年，外加天知道五年、六年、七年的一年期延展。

turns.en: We're looking at a 20 year relationship probably at the end of the day if we continue to re-up and so if your general partners aren't going to be there anymore, if they want to retire or they're just getting really old that they can't participate anymore, you're losing pull or you're losing access to maybe a specific pool of people that's done you really well.
turns.zh: 说到底，如果我们持续续投，那大概是 20 年的关系。所以如果你的普通合伙人不再在这里了——他们想退休，或者只是年纪太大、没法再参与——你就在失去牵引力，或者失去对某一群曾给你带来极大好处的人的触达。

turns.en: So if you have, let's say a GP who was a huge hire up at Google, this is a completely random example and you've been pulling in deep mind founders and you've been attracting the talent that's come out of that company and you were a senior there and people really respect your relationship with that sub-perfect founders and then you're no longer there, maybe you lose your tie to that pool of founders and then they're going to go to somebody else
turns.zh: 所以，比如说你有一位 GP 曾在 Google 是个大人物——这完全是随口举的例子——你一直在把 DeepMind 的创始人拉进来，一直在吸引从那家公司出来的人才，你曾是那里的高管，大家也非常敬重你跟那些创始人的关系；然后你不再待在那儿了，也许你就失去了跟那一群创始人的纽带，他们就会转投别人，

turns.en: that has the same sort of point of similarity or that they can bond over that with and so I think the best way to mitigate that is to really, really promote from within and build up your junior and like principal level investors and help them brand as the firm grows.
turns.zh: 转而投向那个跟他们有相似之处、能就此建立联结的人。所以我觉得缓解这一点的最佳方式，就是真真正正地从内部提拔，培养你的初级和总监级（principal）投资人，随着公司成长帮他们打造个人品牌。

turns.en: But I think that there's been a little bit of lack of investment in that because there's so much focus on the media presence of the firm, the brand itself, which I think is great.
turns.zh: 但我觉得在这方面投入有点不足，因为太多注意力都放在了机构的媒体存在感、品牌本身上——这一点我觉得是好的，

turns.en: I think is super important, but as time goes on and some of your older people start to retire or move away and then I don't recognize a single name on a deck anymore, it's kind of like I really wonder what a founder is going to think when there's no longer this presence of iconic, iconic names that have meant a lot to the firm's history.
turns.zh: 也非常重要，但随着时间推移，当你一些年长的人开始退休或离开，然后我在一份 BP 上一个名字都认不出来时，我就会忍不住想：当那些对机构历史意义重大的标志性名字不再出现时，一位创始人会怎么想？

turns.en: So I think that's been a reason why we've said no to a couple of opportunities that out of first touch I would have been like this is one of the best firms I can possibly think of.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，这就是我们对几个机会说了「不」的原因之一——如果只看第一印象，我本来会觉得：这是我能想到的最好的机构之一，

turns.en: I'm obviously going to say yes, but when they don't really have a really strong succession plan and there is really an indication of that being a focus in the near future, when you're thinking about building a like multi-decade relationship, it just starts to become a point of concern because there are firms that are doing a really great job of that and are pouring a lot into helping to build up their team and make sure that that track is going to
turns.zh: 我当然会点头答应。但当他们并没有一个真正强有力的继任计划、也看不出近期会把这当作重点时，如果你在想建立一段长达数十年的关系，这就开始变成一个隐忧，因为确实有些机构在这方面做得非常好，投入大量资源去帮团队成长、确保这条轨道会

turns.en: stay active and that there is a brand associated not only with them but their people. You mentioned it earlier about how dynamic the market is today.
turns.zh: 持续活跃，确保不仅他们本身、连他们的人都与品牌绑定在一起。——你前面提到如今的市场有多么瞬息万变。

turns.en: We've never seen something like this ever and it actually makes the SaaS era seem pretty archaic in comparison, right? Like I was having this epiphany the other day of like how different was my job in 2017 than 2007 and then how much was my work different in 2007 than 1987?
turns.zh: 我们从没见过这样的局面，跟它一比，SaaS 时代甚至显得相当古老了，对吧？我前几天突然有个感悟：我 2017 年的工作跟 2007 年相比有多大不同，而我 2007 年的工作跟 1987 年相比又有多大不同？

turns.en: Someone doing it. It wasn't. Now things are rapidly changing. People are looking for different things. You can at your fingertips build any SaaS product you want, not that you should but you can.
turns.zh: 对做这行的人来说，其实没那么不同。而现在，事情在飞速变化，人们在寻找不同的东西。你动动手指就能搭建任何你想要的 SaaS 产品——不是说你应该这么做，但你确实能。

turns.en: If all those changing on the ground for founders and then at the passenger seat for the VCs, how does an allocator stay up to date on like what's going on to iterate their own point of view?
turns.zh: 如果这一切在创始人那一端、以及在风投这个「副驾驶座」上都在变化，那么一个配置者要怎么跟上正在发生的事、去迭代自己的观点？

turns.en: Well I think that that is a really important part of the strategy that we employ or just sort of the thesis that we have around what kind of GPs do we want to work with because I think at the end of the day, I mean you've heard it a million times, the distribution is going to be the only mode.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得这是我们采用的策略中非常重要的一部分，或者说就是我们关于「想跟什么样的 GP 合作」的核心论点。因为说到底——我是说这话你已经听过一百万遍了——分发（distribution）将会是唯一的护城河（moat）。

turns.en: If you're building some sort of SaaS or consumer product at this point, obviously it's different if you're talking about hardware or some sort of really specialized industry.
turns.zh: 如果你现在在做某种 SaaS 或消费级产品——当然，如果你说的是硬件或某个非常专门的行业，那就另当别论。

turns.en: That's obviously like a new topic that's a whole different conversation but at the end of the day, if we're going to look for a team that we can trust to build SaaS products or consumer facing products, you need to be with a big fund in my personal opinion.
turns.zh: 那显然是另一个全新的话题、是另一场对话。但说到底，如果我们要找一个信得过的团队去做 SaaS 产品或面向消费者的产品，就我个人的看法，你得背靠一只大基金。

turns.en: That is the mode. Everybody knows that. The opposite is completely true. Where I kind of feel like the real strength for a smaller GP is a really niche specific knowledge around maybe a highly regulated industry or a really complicated one.
turns.zh: 那就是护城河，人人都懂。而反过来则完全成立：我恰恰觉得，规模较小的 GP 的真正强项，是围绕某个高度受监管、或非常复杂的行业的、极其细分的专业知识。

turns.en: I think that you see life sciences and bio, you see hardware, you see anything that relates to selling to the government, you see anything that's tied to blue collar logistics.
turns.zh: 我觉得你会在生命科学和生物科技看到这一点，在硬件看到，在任何跟向政府销售相关的领域看到，在任何跟蓝领物流挂钩的领域看到。

turns.en: I think that smaller GPs can have a really strong pull in that universe so they've got a really niche knowledge because they don't necessarily have to build an insane mode if their product just is that and they have the understanding to be able to deploy to the right places.
turns.zh: 我觉得规模较小的 GP 在这个圈子里可以有很强的牵引力，因为他们拥有非常细分的知识；他们不一定非得打造一个惊人的护城河，如果他们的产品本身就是那种护城河，而且他们有足够的理解力把钱投到对的地方。

turns.en: So with how fast everything is changing, I think that the trust that you have to have this an LP is that we can't predict the future and none of these GPs can either.
turns.zh: 所以在一切都变化得如此之快的当下，我觉得作为 LP，你必须抱有的一种信任是：我们没法预测未来，这些 GP 也一样不能。

turns.en: At the end of the day, no one knows what's going to happen tomorrow. There is no all seeing eye that's going to have the right answers and so if you're making a bet in a riskier area or an area that you feel like is more unstable or potentially changing faster, that's where I feel like it's better to offload that responsibility to people that have so much manpower and brand power that they can will their way through
turns.zh: 说到底，没人知道明天会发生什么。没有一只全知之眼能给出正确答案。所以如果你在一个风险更高的领域、或一个你觉得更不稳定、可能变化更快的领域下注，那么我觉得，更好的做法是把这份责任交给那些人力和品牌力量强大到能够凭意志硬闯过去的人。

turns.en: it. Rachel, you are this incredible dedicated resource for like Lenora Capital clients who is deep in venture. You are, you're talking to the biggest names, you're talking to the hottest new emerging managers.
turns.zh: ……闯过去。Rachel，你是 Lenora Capital 客户们一位了不起的专属资源，深耕风投。你在跟最大的那些名字交谈，也在跟最炙手可热的新兴管理人交谈。

turns.en: What is the thing that your clients are also in some cases the people running Seattle? What, what is the thing that, that like where are people better off making their direct investments?
turns.zh: 你的客户——他们有些其实就是在经营 Seattle 这座城市的人——那么，究竟在哪些方面，人们更适合去做他们的直接投资？

turns.en: I know you're coaching your clients constantly on their own sort of like individual access deals, angel deals, they're getting pitched GP pitches as well.
turns.zh: 我知道你一直在辅导客户处理他们自己的那些个人 access 交易、天使交易，他们也会收到 GP 的推介。

turns.en: Our audience are looking to allocate into this industry and they have some access. They also are maybe considering like a fund of funds or going into a pool of vehicle like yours.
turns.zh: 我们的听众正想把资金配置进这个行业，他们也有一定的触达渠道。他们可能也在考虑一只母基金（fund of funds），或者加入像你们那样的一个汇集型载体。

turns.en: At a high level, where do you see like meeting a middle man and where you can kind of do it yourself? Like there's so much interest in doing direct deals.
turns.zh: 从大的层面上看，你觉得哪里适合借助中间人、哪里又适合亲力亲为？大家对做直接交易（direct deals）有这么多兴趣。

turns.en: What do you, what's your sort of coaching of your clients on what percentage of their capital should be going into your dedicated pots versus the things that they are getting pitched, you know, through friends?
turns.zh: 你会怎么辅导你的客户：他们资本的多少比例应该投进你们那些专属的资金池，又有多少应该投给那些通过朋友之类推介给他们的东西？

turns.en: Yeah, that's a huge part of my job that's completely separate from being like an investor myself and is like a pure coaching experience, which is very unique to have such an impressive set of people send you an email and be like, Hey, what do you think of this?
turns.zh: 是啊，这是我工作中很大的一部分，跟我自己当投资人完全是两码事，纯粹是一种辅导体验。这非常独特——会有这么一群了不起的人给你发邮件说：嘿，你怎么看这个？

turns.en: Does this make sense for me? And so it's, it's different, right? It's very much based on the size of the clients. There are some clients that are so large that at the end of the day, it's important to frame something as like a financial investment versus a passion investment.
turns.zh: 这个对我合适吗？所以这因人而异，对吧？很大程度上取决于客户的规模。有些客户体量非常大，以至于说到底，重要的是把某件事界定为一笔财务投资，还是一笔热情投资。

turns.en: I think that the fund vehicle that we've created is a financial tool. It would take a lot of capital and a lot of time and a lot of dedicated research to build this portfolio because it's not only venture, it's real estate, it's private equity, it's doing direct buyouts, it's buying apartment buildings and senior housing and it's helping to run those things as an individual person.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们创建的这个基金载体是一种财务工具。要搭建这样一个组合，需要大量资本、大量时间和大量专门的研究，因为它不只是风投，还有房地产、私募股权、直接并购，还有买公寓楼、买养老住宅，并帮着运营这些东西——一个人根本做不到。

turns.en: Even if you're the CEO of a company, you don't have the time to do that and do it to the best of your ability. It makes sense to outsource that if you want a diversified allocation to the private markets.
turns.zh: 哪怕你是一家公司的 CEO，你也没有时间去做这些事、并且把它做到你能力的极致。如果你想在私募市场有一个多元化的配置，把它外包出去是合理的。

turns.en: That's where a fee is worth it because you are not going to be able to build that same portfolio on your own time. Even if you wanted to pay your own individual team to do so and you wanted a completely solo family office, that is another huge amount of capital.
turns.zh: 这就是费用值得付的地方，因为你没法靠自己的时间搭建出同样的组合。哪怕你想自己掏钱组一个团队来做、想搞一个完全独立的单一家族办公室，那又是一大笔资本。

turns.en: I really think that in a lot of cases, if you're interested in general private markets exposure and you understand why you want to be invested in the private markets, it makes sense to do a fund-to-fund structure like what we're doing or what somebody else is doing because it takes so much lift off of you and you have a huge set of resources if you're doing that.
turns.zh: 我真的觉得，很多情况下，如果你想要的是对私募市场的整体敞口、也明白自己为什么想投私募市场，那么采用一种母基金式的结构——像我们在做的，或者别人在做的——就是合理的，因为它替你卸掉了大量负担，而且这样做你能拥有一大批资源。

turns.en: So you're paying that fee for a reason at the end of the day, which is to employ a full group of people to go and take care of this investing process for you.
turns.zh: 所以说到底，你付那笔费用是有道理的，那就是雇一整支队伍去替你打理这整个投资流程。

turns.en: It's totally different if you have a passion area that you want to be involved in, if you've got a specific area that you know a lot about. I think we kind of see two fold of this in the venture space.
turns.zh: 但如果你有一个自己想参与的热情领域、有一个你非常了解的特定领域，那情况就完全不同了。我觉得在风投领域，我们看到的是两方面。

turns.en: One is, hey, I have access to this direct deal. It's this round. These are the terms. What should I do? That question is usually way more one of, well, how did you get this opportunity?
turns.zh: 一方面是：嘿，我拿到了这个直接交易的机会，是这一轮，条款是这样，我该怎么做？这个问题其实更多应该变成：好，你是怎么拿到这个机会的？

turns.en: Who brought this to you? Do you feel like you want to be involved with this person? Do you want insight or access just to have like an observer see on what's going on?
turns.zh: 是谁把它带给你的？你觉得自己想跟这个人打交道吗？你是想要洞见或触达，还是只想有一个旁观者视角看看正在发生什么？

turns.en: Are you just really excited about it? Like let's drill down on to why you want to do this opportunity. I have one last question for you, Rachel, why I have you here.
turns.zh: 还是你只是真的对它很兴奋？让我们深挖一下：你为什么要做这个机会。——Rachel，我还有最后一个问题要问你，也是我请你来的原因。

turns.en: Because look through your, you know, look through the future and I want you to give us a prediction on where do you see the media wars going?
turns.zh: 因为请你展望未来，我想让你给我们一个预测：你觉得这场媒体大战（media wars）会走向何方？

turns.en: What is the like, in venture? Like is it something that we just forget? Is it something that's going to be lasting? Just what do you think this whole kind of like media wars, what it does?
turns.zh: 在风投里，这到底是什么？是那种我们转头就忘的东西，还是会长期存在的东西？你觉得这整场媒体大战，它究竟会带来什么？

turns.en: Well, I have a unique lens into this. My sister works in commercial production and she has worked with a couple of awesome startups and that's a universe that I don't really touch at all.
turns.zh: 嗯，我对这件事有一个独特的视角。我妹妹做商业影视制作，她跟几家很棒的初创公司合作过，而那是一个我完全不涉足的领域。

turns.en: So I get to see another side of what does it look like to produce a lot of this content and how much money is going into it. Not only on the behalf of venture teams themselves, but like underlying portfolio companies.
turns.zh: 所以我能看到另一面：制作这么多内容是什么样子、往里砸了多少钱——不只是风投团队自己出的钱，还有他们底层的被投公司。

turns.en: I think it's going to be everything. It's the streaming wars, it's the entertainmentification of the entire economy. We talk a lot about how perhaps even one day we're going to see talent looking a lot more so like sports talent in tech than it does currently where you have maybe even an agent that's helping to negotiate offers between different massive companies.
turns.zh: 我觉得它会是一切。这是流媒体大战，是整个经济的「娱乐化」。我们经常谈到，也许有一天，科技行业的人才会越来越像体育界的人才——甚至比现在更像——你甚至会有一位经纪人，帮你在不同的大公司之间谈判报价。

turns.en: And I see that the kind of circle meeting at the top again, like we talked about earlier is going to come true with entertainment and with venture.
turns.zh: 而且我看到，那种「圈子在顶端重新交汇」——就像我们前面聊到的——将会在娱乐和风投之间成真。

turns.en: It's how you get eyes on your portfolio companies. It's not only how you get customers, but it's how you get talent and it's how you retain talent and I think that that is so, so, so difficult to do and having talent retention not only as a startup with your underlying portfolio companies, but also as a general partner is completely make or break to your ability to succeed.
turns.zh: 它是你让大家的目光聚焦到你被投公司上的方式。它不只是你获取客户的方式，也是你吸引人才、留住人才的方式。我觉得这件事非常非常非常难做，而人才留存——不仅对作为初创公司的被投企业，也对普通合伙人而言——完全决定了你能否成功。

turns.en: And so having those eyes on you, it brings you more money. It brings you more LPs. It brings you better founders. It wins you deals at more disciplined prices.
turns.zh: 所以有这些目光聚焦在你身上，会给你带来更多钱、更多 LP、更好的创始人，还能让你以更自律的价格拿下交易。

turns.en: It helps you attract better talents to make those investment decisions. It helps you attract better talent for your underlying portfolio companies because at the end of the day, people like eyeballs on them if they've got ambitious goals and that is what's going to win.
turns.zh: 它帮你吸引更优秀的人才来做那些投资决策，也帮你为底层的被投公司吸引更优秀的人才。因为说到底，如果一个人有远大的目标，他就喜欢有目光聚焦在自己身上——而这才是制胜之道。

turns.en: I think that we're going to continue to see podcasts, sub-stack, YouTube. I think about startup launch videos that have become so popular. I think that's going to become even more extreme.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们会继续看到播客、Substack、YouTube。我会想到那些已经非常流行的初创公司产品发布视频，我觉得那还会变得更加极致。

turns.en: You think about iconic movies that have to do with the tech scene that have stood up over time. The social network is not the last of its kind.
turns.zh: 你想想那些与科技圈有关、经受住时间考验的经典电影。《社交网络》（The Social Network）绝不是最后一部这类电影。

turns.en: I wouldn't be surprised before we see some sort of 816Z documentary get dropped. And so I think that the media awards are going to continue to be a huge, huge, huge, if not increasingly larger part of what makes a firm attractive and what keeps them around.
turns.zh: 如果哪天我们看到某种关于 a16z 的纪录片上线，我一点也不会惊讶。所以我觉得，媒体大战将会继续成为——甚至越来越大的一部分——决定一家机构是否有吸引力、能否长久存在的因素。

turns.en: And I think as things get really, really volatile, the ability to control your own narrative is so, so important. And if you have a ton of owned media channels, you can do that and you can stand on the ground of your thesis and you can stand on the ground of what you're doing.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得，当局势变得非常非常动荡时，掌控自己叙事的能力就变得极其重要。如果你有大量自有媒体渠道（owned media），你就能做到这一点，就能站在你自己的投资论点、站在你正在做的事情这块地基上。

turns.en: And if you have people listening to you and not listening to a news outlet writing something about you or about your industry, that's everything.
turns.zh: 如果有人愿意听你说，而不是去听某个新闻媒体写关于你或你所在行业的报道，那就是一切。

turns.en: So I think it's not just media, but it's owned media. It's media that you have control over and people are looking to you first to hear about what you're doing rather than looking elsewhere.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，这不只是媒体，而是自有媒体——是你能够掌控的媒体，是人们会先来听你讲你在做什么，而不是去别处找。

turns.en: I think it's going to be make or break. So I'm very excited about that. I think it's a completely new turn for the industry and we're short of at the beginning of it.
turns.zh: 我觉得这将是成败关键。所以我对此非常兴奋。我认为这是行业一个全新的转折，而我们才刚刚站在它的起点上。

turns.en: And so I'm very curious to see how that changes over time. Thanks so much, Rachel. That's awesome. Of course. Thanks, Rachel. So nice to talk to you guys.
turns.zh: 所以我很好奇它会随时间如何演变。——非常感谢你，Rachel，太精彩了。——不客气。——谢谢你，Rachel，很高兴和你们聊。
